subject: biology
overview: Plant Physiology explains how plants capture light energy through photosynthesis, release that energy through respiration, and grow and develop under the control of internal and external factors, including plant growth regulators. It is a high-weightage NEET unit. Questions test numbers (ATP, turns of the Calvin cycle, RQ), sites of reactions, enzymes, the C3 versus C4 comparison, growth-rate calculations and practical uses of PGRs.

topics.explanation: Photosynthesis is a physico-chemical process in which green plants use light energy to make organic compounds from $CO_2$ and water. This makes them autotrophs, and nearly all life on earth depends on them for food and oxygen. Our understanding grew through a series of classic experiments. Priestley (1770) showed that air is restored by plants. Ingenhousz showed that sunlight and green parts are needed. Sachs (1854) showed that glucose is produced and stored as starch. Engelmann obtained the first action spectrum using Cladophora and aerobic bacteria. Van Niel proved that $O_2$ comes from water. Photosynthesis occurs mainly in the mesophyll cells of leaves, inside chloroplasts. The membrane system (grana and thylakoids) traps light and makes ATP and NADPH. The stroma contains the enzymes that reduce $CO_2$ to sugar.
key_points: Autotrophic nutrition is seen only in plants, algae and some bacteria.
Priestley used a bell jar, a candle, a mouse and a mint plant to show that plants restore bad air.
Ingenhousz showed that only the green parts of plants, in sunlight, release oxygen.
Sachs showed that glucose is made and is usually stored as starch.
Engelmann used a prism and found that bacteria gathered in blue and red light, giving the first action spectrum.
Van Niel, working with purple and green bacteria, showed that $O_2$ released by green plants comes from $H_2O$, not $CO_2$.
Chloroplasts line up along mesophyll cell walls for optimum light.
Thylakoids (grana) carry out the light reaction; the stroma carries out the dark (biosynthetic) reaction.

formulas.meaning: Overall equation of photosynthesis; it shows that the oxygen released comes from water.
Van Niel's general equation, where $H_2A$ is the oxidisable hydrogen donor.

topics.neet_tip: NEET asks the chronological sequence of experiments: Priestley, then Ingenhousz, then Sachs, then Engelmann, then van Niel.
topics.topic: Photosynthesis as autotrophic nutrition; site of photosynthesis

topics.explanation: Paper chromatography of leaf pigments separates four pigments. Chlorophyll a is bright or blue-green. Chlorophyll b is yellow-green. Xanthophylls are yellow. Carotenoids are yellow to yellow-orange. Chlorophyll a is the chief pigment and forms the reaction centre. The absorption spectrum of chlorophyll a shows peaks in the blue and red regions. The action spectrum of photosynthesis closely matches this absorption spectrum. This shows that most photosynthesis takes place in blue and red light. The other pigments are accessory pigments. They absorb a wider range of wavelengths and pass the energy to chlorophyll a. They also protect chlorophyll a from photo-oxidation.
key_points: Chlorophyll a is the main pigment and is present at both reaction centres, P680 and P700.
Accessory pigments are chlorophyll b, xanthophylls and carotenoids.
Maximum absorption and photosynthesis occur in the blue and red regions of the spectrum.
Some photosynthesis also occurs in other wavelengths because accessory pigments absorb them.
Accessory pigments protect chlorophyll a from photo-oxidation.
Photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) is 400 to 700 nm.
topics.neet_tip: Expect questions on the colour of each pigment in chromatography and on which pigment forms the P700 or P680 reaction centre (chlorophyll a).

topics.explanation: Photosynthesis has two phases. The photochemical (light) phase takes place on the thylakoid membranes. It includes light absorption, splitting of water, release of oxygen, and formation of ATP and NADPH. Pigments are organised into two light harvesting complexes, PS I and PS II. Each has a reaction centre surrounded by antenna pigments. The biosynthetic phase (Calvin cycle, or C3 cycle) takes place in the stroma. It uses that ATP and NADPH to fix $CO_2$ into carbohydrate. The biosynthetic phase is not directly light-driven but depends on the products of the light phase. Melvin Calvin used radioactive $^{14}C$ in algae and found that the first stable product is 3-phosphoglyceric acid (PGA). The cycle has three stages. Carboxylation of RuBP is done by RuBisCO. Reduction converts PGA to triose phosphate. Regeneration rebuilds RuBP.
key_points: Water splitting is associated with PS II on the inner (lumen) side of the thylakoid membrane.
Water splitting requires $Mn^{2+}$ and $Cl^-$.
The Z-scheme of electron flow runs PS II, then the electron transport chain, then PS I, then $NADP^+$.
The $CO_2$ acceptor is RuBP (5C); the first stable product is 3-PGA (3C).
RuBisCO is the most abundant enzyme in the world.
Fixing one $CO_2$ needs 3 ATP and 2 NADPH.
Forming one glucose needs 6 turns of the cycle, 18 ATP and 12 NADPH.
The cycle runs in all photosynthetic plants, both C3 and C4.

formulas.meaning: Photolysis of water at PS II; it supplies electrons to replace those lost by P680.
Example: 3 glucose molecules need 18 turns of the Calvin cycle.
Energy requirement for making one glucose molecule.

topics.neet_tip: Numerical questions on Calvin cycle turns, ATP and NADPH requirement are very common; remember 6 turns, 18 ATP and 12 NADPH per glucose.
topics.topic: Photochemical and biosynthetic phases of photosynthesis

topics.explanation: Photophosphorylation is the synthesis of ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate in the presence of light. In non-cyclic photophosphorylation, PS II and PS I work in series. Electrons flow from water through PS II and PS I to $NADP^+$. This produces ATP, NADPH and $O_2$, and it occurs in the grana thylakoids. In cyclic photophosphorylation, only PS I works. Excited electrons from P700 return to the same PS I through the electron transport chain. Only ATP is formed; no NADPH and no $O_2$ are produced. It occurs in the stroma lamellae. These lack PS II and the NADP reductase enzyme. Cyclic flow also operates when only light of wavelength beyond 680 nm is available.
key_points: Non-cyclic photophosphorylation uses PS II and PS I and produces ATP, NADPH and $O_2$.
Cyclic photophosphorylation uses PS I only and produces ATP only.
Stroma lamellae lack PS II and NADP reductase, so only cyclic flow occurs there.
The reaction centre of PS I is P700; that of PS II is P680.
In the Z-scheme, electrons from PS II pass down the chain to PS I.
The final electron acceptor in non-cyclic flow is $NADP^+$.
topics.neet_tip: NEET often asks the site of cyclic photophosphorylation (stroma lamellae) and which products it lacks (NADPH and $O_2$).

topics.explanation: Mitchell's chemiosmotic hypothesis explains how ATP is made. A proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane drives ATP synthesis. Protons build up in the lumen in three ways. First, water splitting releases $H^+$ inside the lumen. Second, the electron carrier moves protons from the stroma into the lumen as electrons travel through the chain. Third, NADP reductase on the stroma side removes $H^+$ from the stroma while reducing $NADP^+$. The result is a high proton concentration in the lumen and a lower pH there. Protons then flow back to the stroma through the $CF_0$ channel of ATP synthase. This flow changes the shape of $CF_1$, which makes ATP on the stroma side. In mitochondria, protons instead accumulate in the intermembrane space.
key_points: ATP synthase has two parts: $CF_0$ is the transmembrane proton channel and $CF_1$ projects into the stroma.
ATP and NADPH are released into the stroma, where the Calvin cycle uses them.
The proton gradient is broken down by the flow of $H^+$ through $CF_0$.
Chemiosmosis needs a membrane, a proton pump, a proton gradient and ATP synthase.
In mitochondria the equivalent parts of ATP synthase (Complex V) are $F_0$ and $F_1$.
topics.neet_tip: Questions ask where protons accumulate (lumen in chloroplast, intermembrane space in mitochondria) and which part of ATP synthase forms the channel ($F_0$).

topics.explanation: RuBisCO can bind both $CO_2$ and $O_2$, and its affinity for $CO_2$ is higher. When $O_2$ concentration is high, RuBP combines with $O_2$ instead of $CO_2$. This oxygenation gives one molecule of 3-PGA and one molecule of 2-phosphoglycolate, in place of two PGA molecules. The pathway involves three organelles: chloroplast, peroxisome and mitochondria. It releases $CO_2$ and produces no ATP or NADPH. Instead, it consumes ATP, so it is a wasteful process that lowers C3 productivity. Photorespiration occurs in C3 plants. It is absent in C4 plants because they concentrate $CO_2$ around RuBisCO in the bundle sheath cells.
key_points: Photorespiration is the oxygenase activity of RuBisCO.
Its products are 3-PGA (3C) and phosphoglycolate (2C).
No sugar, ATP or NADPH is formed; $O_2$ is used and $CO_2$ is released.
It involves the chloroplast, peroxisome and mitochondria.
It is common in C3 plants, especially at high temperature and high $O_2$.
It is absent in C4 plants, which is a reason for their higher productivity.

formulas.meaning: Oxygenation reaction of RuBisCO, the first step of photorespiration.
Normal carboxylation reaction, given for comparison.

topics.neet_tip: Statement-based questions test that photorespiration occurs in C3 plants, forms phosphoglycolate, and produces no ATP or NADPH.

topics.explanation: C3 plants fix $CO_2$ directly through the Calvin cycle in mesophyll cells. Their first stable product is 3-PGA, a 3-carbon compound. C4 plants, such as maize, sorghum, sugarcane and Amaranthus, are adapted to dry tropical regions. They show Kranz anatomy, in which large bundle sheath cells with many chloroplasts surround the vascular bundles. This is the Hatch and Slack pathway. In mesophyll cells, PEP (3C) accepts $CO_2$ using PEP carboxylase (PEPcase), which has no oxygenase activity. This forms oxaloacetic acid (OAA, 4C). OAA is converted to malate or aspartate, which moves to the bundle sheath. There it is decarboxylated to release $CO_2$ for the Calvin cycle. The remaining 3C molecule returns to the mesophyll and PEP is regenerated.
key_points: The primary $CO_2$ acceptor is RuBP in C3 plants and PEP in C4 plants.
The first stable product is 3-PGA in C3 plants and OAA in C4 plants.
Mesophyll cells of C4 plants lack RuBisCO.
Bundle sheath cells of C4 plants lack PEPcase.
Bundle sheath cells have thick walls that are impervious to gases, and no intercellular spaces.
The Calvin cycle occurs in the bundle sheath cells of C4 plants.
C4 plants tolerate higher temperatures and have a higher temperature optimum.
C4 plants have high productivity because they lack photorespiration.

formulas.meaning: Primary carboxylation in C4 mesophyll cells.

topics.neet_tip: Comparison questions are frequent: the location of RuBisCO versus PEPcase, first products, Kranz anatomy, and examples of C4 plants.

topics.explanation: Photosynthesis is affected by internal factors and external factors. Internal factors include the number, size, age and orientation of leaves, mesophyll cells and chloroplasts, and the internal $CO_2$ concentration. External factors include light, $CO_2$, temperature and water. Blackman's law of limiting factors (1905) says the following. If a chemical process depends on several factors, its rate is set by the factor nearest its minimal value. A change in that factor alone will change the rate. Light saturation occurs at about 10% of full sunlight. $CO_2$ is the major limiting factor in nature because air contains only about 0.03 to 0.04% $CO_2$. C4 plants saturate at about 360 $\mu L/L$ $CO_2$. C3 plants keep responding to higher $CO_2$ concentrations.
key_points: Light is rarely limiting in nature, except for plants in shade or dense forests.
Very high light intensity causes chlorophyll breakdown.
Increasing $CO_2$ up to 0.05% raises the rate of $CO_2$ fixation.
Greenhouse crops such as tomato and bell pepper are grown in $CO_2$-enriched air for higher yield.
Dark reactions are enzymatic and therefore sensitive to temperature.
Water stress closes stomata and causes leaves to wilt, so it affects photosynthesis indirectly.
C3 plants have a lower temperature optimum than C4 plants.
topics.neet_tip: Expect questions on Blackman's law, the main limiting factor ($CO_2$), and the $CO_2$ response of C3 versus C4 plants.

topics.explanation: Respiration is the breakdown of C-C bonds of complex organic molecules by oxidation, which releases energy that is trapped as ATP. Plants have no specialised respiratory organs. Gas exchange occurs by diffusion through stomata and lenticels. This is enough for three reasons. Each plant part takes care of its own gas-exchange needs, with little transport between parts. Plants have a low demand for gas exchange compared with animals. The distance gases must diffuse is short, because most living cells are close to the surface. In stems the living cells form thin layers beneath the bark, with lenticels, and the inner cells are dead. Leaves also produce $O_2$ during photosynthesis, which they can use for respiration.
key_points: Gas exchange takes place through stomata in leaves and lenticels in stems.
Roots, stems and leaves respire at much lower rates than animals.
Loosely packed parenchyma creates an interconnected network of air spaces.
Glucose is the most common respiratory substrate.
The energy released is stored in ATP, the energy currency of the cell.
topics.neet_tip: NEET asks why plants survive without special respiratory organs; the reasons are low demand, short diffusion distance, and each part managing its own gas exchange.

topics.explanation: Glycolysis, also called the EMP pathway after Embden, Meyerhof and Parnas, occurs in the cytoplasm of all living organisms. It is the only process of respiration in anaerobes. One glucose (6C) is broken into two molecules of pyruvic acid (3C). ATP is used at two steps: glucose to glucose-6-phosphate (hexokinase) and fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (phosphofructokinase). ATP is formed directly at two steps: BPGA to 3-PGA and PEP to pyruvate. Two NADH are formed when PGAL is converted to BPGA. The net gain is 2 ATP and 2 NADH per glucose. Without $O_2$, pyruvate undergoes fermentation. In yeast, alcoholic fermentation produces ethanol and $CO_2$ using pyruvate decarboxylase and alcohol dehydrogenase. In muscle cells and some bacteria, lactate dehydrogenase forms lactic acid. Fermentation regenerates $NAD^+$ but releases less than 7% of the energy in glucose.
key_points: Glycolysis gives 2 pyruvate per glucose; for example, 206 glucose give 412 pyruvate.
Glycolysis uses 2 ATP and makes 4 ATP, a net gain of 2 ATP.
Sucrose is first split by invertase into glucose and fructose.
The reducing agent in fermentation is NADH, which is reoxidised to $NAD^+$.
Yeasts poison themselves when the alcohol concentration reaches about 13%.
Fermentation gives a net gain of only 2 ATP.

formulas.meaning: Number of pyruvate molecules formed at the end of glycolysis.

topics.neet_tip: NEET asks simple numericals on pyruvate formed, the enzymes of fermentation, and the steps where ATP is used or formed.

topics.explanation: Pyruvate enters the mitochondrial matrix. There, pyruvate dehydrogenase converts it to acetyl CoA, releasing $CO_2$ and forming NADH; this needs $Mg^{2+}$, $NAD^+$ and coenzyme A. The TCA (Krebs or citric acid) cycle starts when acetyl CoA (2C) condenses with OAA (4C) and water to form citric acid (6C). This step is catalysed by citrate synthase. Each turn gives 2 $CO_2$, 3 NADH, 1 $FADH_2$ and 1 GTP or ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation. The cycle turns twice per glucose. In the electron transport system (ETS) on the inner mitochondrial membrane, electrons pass through a series of complexes: Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase), ubiquinone, Complex III (cytochrome $bc_1$), cytochrome c, and Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase). Electrons from $FADH_2$ enter through Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase). Oxygen is the final acceptor and forms water. Complex V (ATP synthase) makes ATP by oxidative phosphorylation.
key_points: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm; link reaction and TCA cycle in the matrix; ETS on the inner membrane.
The TCA cycle requires continued regeneration of OAA.
Cytochrome c is a small protein attached to the outer surface of the inner membrane; it carries electrons from Complex III to IV.
Complex IV contains cytochromes a and $a_3$ and two copper centres.
$F_1$ is the peripheral headpiece where ATP is made.
$F_0$ is the integral membrane part that forms the proton channel.
Oxygen acts at the end of the chain as the final hydrogen acceptor, but it drives the whole process.

formulas.formula: $\text{Pyruvic acid} + CoA + NAD^+ \rightarrow \text{Acetyl CoA} + CO_2 + NADH + H^+$
formulas.meaning: Link reaction catalysed by pyruvate dehydrogenase.

topics.neet_tip: Questions focus on the site of each step, the names of the complexes, the role of cytochrome c and ubiquinone, and the products per TCA turn.
topics.topic: TCA cycle and electron transport system

topics.explanation: Theoretical ATP yield is calculated with these assumptions: a sequential, orderly pathway; NADH from glycolysis enters the mitochondria; no intermediates are withdrawn; only glucose is the substrate. Each NADH gives 3 ATP and each $FADH_2$ gives 2 ATP. Glycolysis gives a net 2 ATP plus 2 NADH, which equals 6 ATP. The link reaction gives 2 NADH, which equals 6 ATP. Two turns of the TCA cycle give 6 NADH (18 ATP), 2 $FADH_2$ (4 ATP) and 2 GTP or ATP. The total is 38 ATP per glucose in aerobic respiration. In fermentation the net gain is only 2 ATP per glucose. In reality pathways work simultaneously and intermediates are withdrawn, so the 38 ATP figure is theoretical.
key_points: Aerobic respiration gives a net 38 ATP per glucose (theoretical).
Anaerobic respiration or fermentation gives a net 2 ATP.
Substrate-level ATP per glucose is 4 (glycolysis) plus 2 (TCA cycle).
Per glucose, 10 NADH and 2 $FADH_2$ are formed.
Glucose is completely oxidised to 6 $CO_2$, released at the link reaction and in the TCA cycle.

formulas.meaning: The 10 NADH give 30 ATP and the 2 $FADH_2$ give 4 ATP. Adding 4 substrate-level ATP from glycolysis and 2 from the TCA cycle, and subtracting the 2 ATP used in glycolysis, gives 38.

topics.neet_tip: NEET asks the net ATP from aerobic versus anaerobic respiration and ATP from a given number of NADH or $FADH_2$.
topics.topic: Energy relations: number of ATP molecules generated

topics.explanation: Respiration is better called an amphibolic pathway than a purely catabolic one, because it takes part in both breakdown and synthesis. Substrates other than glucose enter at different points. Fats break into glycerol, which becomes PGAL, and fatty acids, which become acetyl CoA. Proteins break into amino acids, which are deaminated and enter as pyruvate, acetyl CoA or Krebs cycle intermediates. During synthesis, intermediates are withdrawn from the pathway. For example, acetyl CoA is used to make fatty acids, and Krebs intermediates are used to make amino acids. Breakdown and synthesis are therefore linked through a common pool of intermediates.
key_points: Glycerol enters respiration as PGAL (3-phosphoglyceraldehyde).
Fatty acids enter as acetyl CoA.
Amino acids enter after deamination, at pyruvate, acetyl CoA or the Krebs cycle.
Fatty acid synthesis withdraws acetyl CoA from the respiratory pathway.
Amphibolic means both catabolic and anabolic.
topics.neet_tip: Questions ask the entry point of glycerol, fatty acids or amino acids, and why respiration is called amphibolic.

topics.explanation: The respiratory quotient (RQ), or respiratory ratio, is the ratio of the volume of $CO_2$ evolved to the volume of $O_2$ consumed during respiration. It depends on the respiratory substrate. For carbohydrates, which are completely oxidised, RQ is 1. For fats it is less than 1, about 0.7, because fats contain little oxygen and need more $O_2$ for oxidation. For proteins it is about 0.9. Organic acids have an RQ greater than 1. In anaerobic respiration $CO_2$ is evolved but no $O_2$ is consumed, so RQ is infinite.
key_points: RQ is 1 for carbohydrates.
RQ is about 0.7 for fats; tripalmitin gives $102/145 = 0.7$.
RQ is about 0.9 for proteins.
RQ is greater than 1 for organic acids such as malic and oxalic acid.
RQ is infinite in anaerobic respiration.

formulas.formula: $RQ = \frac{\text{volume of } CO_2 \text{ evolved}}{\text{volume of } O_2 \text{ consumed}}$
formulas.meaning: Used to identify the respiratory substrate.
Oxidation of tripalmitin, a fat; RQ = 0.7.

topics.neet_tip: Expect direct RQ values for different substrates or a calculation from a given balanced equation.

topics.explanation: Seed germination is the process by which the embryo resumes growth and forms a seedling. It is the first step of a plant's post-embryonic growth. Germination needs suitable conditions: water, oxygen and a favourable temperature, and light in some seeds. Imbibition of water swells the seed and activates enzymes. Stored food is broken down and respiration supplies energy. The radicle emerges first, followed by the plumule. Seeds that fail to germinate even under favourable external conditions are dormant. Dormancy is caused by endogenous factors such as a hard seed coat, chemical inhibitors like abscisic acid, or an immature embryo. Dormancy can be broken by gibberellins, chilling, scarification or changes in light and temperature.
key_points: Germination requires water, $O_2$ and a suitable temperature.
Imbibition is the first step of germination.
The radicle emerges before the plumule.
Gibberellins promote germination and break dormancy.
ABA induces seed dormancy and inhibits germination.
Ethylene promotes germination, for example in peanut seeds.
Dormancy is controlled internally; quiescence is due only to unfavourable external conditions.
topics.neet_tip: NEET usually links germination to PGRs: GA and ethylene promote it, ABA inhibits it.

topics.explanation: Growth is an irreversible, permanent increase in the size of an organ, its parts or a cell. Plant growth is indeterminate, or open, because meristems keep dividing. At a root or shoot tip, growth occurs in three phases. The meristematic phase has dividing cells with dense protoplasm and large nuclei. In the elongation phase, cells enlarge, become vacuolated and lay down new walls. In the maturation phase, cells reach maximum size and differentiate. In arithmetic growth, only one daughter cell keeps dividing, which gives a linear curve. In geometric growth, both daughter cells divide, which gives a sigmoid curve with a lag phase, a log (exponential) phase and a stationary phase. Absolute growth rate is the total growth per unit time. Relative growth rate is the growth per unit time per unit of initial size.
key_points: Growth is measured by increase in fresh weight, dry weight, length, area, volume or cell number.
A maize root apical meristem produces more than 17,500 new cells per hour.
Watermelon cells may increase in size up to 350,000 times.
Pollen tube growth is measured by length; dorsiventral leaf growth by surface area.
Arithmetic growth gives a straight line; geometric growth gives a sigmoid (S-shaped) curve.
In the geometric formula, r is the relative growth rate, also called the efficiency index.
Two leaves can have the same absolute growth rate but different relative growth rates.

formulas.meaning: Arithmetic growth. Example: $L_0 = 20$ cm, $r = 30$ cm/day, $t = 7$ days gives $L_t = 230$ cm.
Geometric or exponential growth, where r is the relative growth rate and e is the base of natural logarithms.
Relative growth rate per unit time.

topics.neet_tip: NEET sets direct numericals using $L_t = L_0 + rt$ and asks about the phases of the sigmoid curve.
topics.topic: Phases of plant growth and plant growth rate

topics.explanation: Growth needs several essential conditions. Water keeps cells turgid for enlargement and provides the medium for enzyme activity. Oxygen is needed to release metabolic energy through respiration. Nutrients, both macro and micro essential elements, are needed to make protoplasm and act as an energy source. Each plant has an optimum temperature range for growth, and deviation from it can be harmful. Environmental signals such as light and gravity also affect certain phases or stages of growth.
key_points: Turgidity due to water is essential for cell extension.
Respiration supplies the ATP used for growth.
Temperature affects growth through enzyme activity.
Light and gravity act as environmental signals that influence growth.
topics.neet_tip: Usually asked as a simple statement question on why water, $O_2$ and nutrients are needed for growth.

topics.explanation: Cells from the root apical meristem, shoot apical meristem and cambium differentiate and mature to perform specific functions. This is differentiation. For example, tracheary elements lose their protoplasm and develop strong, lignified secondary walls. Living differentiated cells that have lost the ability to divide can regain it under certain conditions; this is dedifferentiation. Interfascicular cambium and cork cambium arise from fully differentiated parenchyma cells. Cells produced by these meristems lose the ability to divide again and mature into specific types; this is redifferentiation. Examples are secondary xylem, secondary phloem and cork. Plants follow different pathways in response to environment and life phase, which is called plasticity. Heterophylly in cotton, coriander and larkspur is an example.
key_points: Differentiation in plants is open: cells from the same meristem can form different structures.
Dedifferentiation produces interfascicular cambium and cork cambium.
Redifferentiation produces secondary xylem, secondary phloem and cork cells.
Heterophylly due to developmental phase is seen in cotton, coriander and larkspur.
Heterophylly due to environment is seen in buttercup (aquatic versus aerial leaves).
Tumour or callus formation in tissue culture involves dedifferentiation.
topics.neet_tip: Matching questions pair interfascicular cambium with dedifferentiation and secondary xylem with redifferentiation, and test heterophylly examples.

topics.explanation: Development covers all the changes an organism goes through during its life cycle, from germination of the seed to senescence. In a plant cell the sequence is as follows. A meristematic cell divides. It undergoes plasmatic growth, meaning an increase in protoplasm. It then expands or elongates. It differentiates, matures and finally undergoes senescence and death. Development is the sum of growth and differentiation. Both intrinsic factors and extrinsic factors control it. Intrinsic factors are internal genetic factors and plant growth regulators. Extrinsic factors are light, temperature, water, oxygen and nutrition.
key_points: Sequence: cell division, plasmatic growth, expansion (elongation), differentiation, maturation, senescence, death.
Development = growth + differentiation.
Intrinsic control comes from genes and PGRs.
Extrinsic control comes from light, temperature, water, oxygen and nutrition.
topics.neet_tip: NEET may ask the correct order of developmental events in a plant cell.
topics.topic: Sequence of developmental process in a plant cell

topics.explanation: PGRs are simple molecules that act as growth promoters or inhibitors. Auxins (IAA, IBA; synthetic NAA, 2,4-D) trace to Darwin's work on canary grass phototropism and Went's isolation from oat coleoptile tips. They promote rooting, apical dominance, parthenocarpy and xylem differentiation; 2,4-D kills dicot weeds. Gibberellins (over 100 forms, GA3 most studied) were discovered by Kurosawa from Gibberella fujikuroi (bakanae disease of rice). They cause stem elongation, bolting, malting and longer grape stalks. Cytokinins, discovered as kinetin from autoclaved herring sperm DNA by Skoog and Miller, are synthesised in regions of rapid cell division, e.g. root apices, developing shoot buds and young fruits, promote cell division and delay senescence. Ethylene, a gas found by Cousins, ripens fruit and promotes senescence. ABA, a stress hormone, closes stomata and induces dormancy.
key_points: Auxin uses: rooting of stem cuttings; flowering in pineapple; preventing fruit and leaf drop at early stages; promoting abscission of older parts; apical dominance; parthenocarpy in tomato; 2,4-D as a dicot weedicide.
Removing the shoot tip (decapitation) is used in tea plantations and hedge-making to remove apical dominance.
GA uses: longer grape stalks; elongated, well-shaped apples; delayed senescence; faster malting in brewing.
GA sprayed on sugarcane increases stem length and yield by up to 20 tonnes per acre.
GA hastens maturity and early seed production in conifers.
GA causes bolting (internode elongation before flowering) in beet, cabbage and rosette plants.
Natural cytokinins such as zeatin come from corn kernels and coconut milk.
Cytokinin effects: new leaves, chloroplasts, lateral shoot and adventitious shoot growth; overcoming apical dominance; nutrient mobilisation.
Ethylene effects: horizontal seedling growth, axis swelling, apical hook; abscission; climacteric respiration rise during ripening.
Ethylene breaks seed and bud dormancy (peanut seeds, potato tubers) and elongates petioles and internodes in deep-water rice.
Ethylene induces flowering in mango, induces female flowers in cucumber, and promotes root hair formation.
Ethephon, which releases ethylene, is the most widely used source of ethylene.
ABA is also known as inhibitor-B, abscission II and dormin.
ABA closes stomata, induces seed dormancy, increases stress tolerance and antagonises GA.
topics.neet_tip: Very high-yield: match each PGR with its discoverer, source or practical use, such as 2,4-D herbicide, GA bolting in cabbage, ethephon ripening, and ABA stomatal closure.
topics.topic: Plant growth regulators: auxin, gibberellin, cytokinin, ethylene and ABA

key_facts: Reaction centre of PS I is P700 and of PS II is P680; both are chlorophyll a.
Water splitting occurs at PS II on the lumen side and needs $Mn^{2+}$ and $Cl^-$.
Cyclic photophosphorylation occurs in the stroma lamellae and produces only ATP.
One glucose needs 6 Calvin cycle turns, 18 ATP and 12 NADPH; 3 glucose need 18 turns.
Fixing one $CO_2$ in the Calvin cycle needs 3 ATP and 2 NADPH.
First stable product: 3-PGA in C3 plants and OAA in C4 plants.
C4 examples: maize, sorghum, sugarcane, Amaranthus.
RuBisCO is the most abundant enzyme on earth.
Photorespiration forms phosphoglycolate and uses chloroplast, peroxisome and mitochondria.
Light saturation occurs at about 10% of full sunlight.
C4 plants are $CO_2$-saturated at about 360 $\mu L/L$.
Glycolysis was worked out by Embden, Meyerhof and Parnas; it gives net 2 ATP, 2 NADH and 2 pyruvate per glucose.
Yeast alcoholic fermentation uses pyruvate decarboxylase and alcohol dehydrogenase; yeast dies at about 13% alcohol.
Citrate synthase condenses acetyl CoA (2C) and OAA (4C) to form citric acid (6C).
Each TCA turn gives 3 NADH, 1 $FADH_2$, 1 GTP and 2 $CO_2$.
Complex IV, cytochrome c oxidase, contains cytochromes a and $a_3$ and two copper centres.
Aerobic respiration gives a net 38 ATP per glucose (theoretical); fermentation gives 2 ATP.
RQ: carbohydrate 1, fat 0.7, protein 0.9, anaerobic respiration infinite.
Arithmetic growth follows $L_t = L_0 + rt$; geometric growth follows $W_1 = W_0 e^{rt}$.
The sigmoid growth curve has lag, log and stationary phases.
Kinetin is a modified adenine (purine) discovered by Skoog and Miller.
Gibberellin was discovered by E. Kurosawa from Gibberella fujikuroi, which causes bakanae disease of rice.
Auxin was first isolated by F.W. Went from oat coleoptile tips; Darwin worked on canary grass.
2,4-D is a selective weedicide that kills dicot weeds.
Ethephon is the most widely used source of ethylene; ethylene induces female flowers in cucumber.
Sugarcane sprayed with GA yields up to 20 tonnes more per acre.
ABA closes stomata and is called the stress hormone.
common_traps: Thinking the oxygen in photosynthesis comes from $CO_2$. It comes from photolysis of water.
Believing photorespiration produces ATP. It actually consumes ATP and produces neither ATP nor NADPH, and it releases $CO_2$.
Saying the Calvin cycle is absent in C4 plants. It occurs in their bundle sheath cells; only the mesophyll cells lack RuBisCO.
Counting pyruvate as equal to glucose. Each glucose gives 2 pyruvate, so n glucose give 2n pyruvate.
Confusing turns per glucose. One turn fixes one $CO_2$, so one glucose needs 6 turns, not 1.
Putting ATP synthase $CF_1$ in the lumen. $CF_1$ faces the stroma, and protons accumulate in the lumen.
Taking dedifferentiation as forming secondary xylem. Secondary xylem is redifferentiation; interfascicular and cork cambium arise by dedifferentiation.
Assuming RQ of fat is greater than 1. Fats need more $O_2$, so their RQ is about 0.7.
quick_revision: Chloroplast: grana carry out the light reaction; the stroma carries out the Calvin cycle.
Non-cyclic flow (PS II plus PS I) gives ATP, NADPH and $O_2$; cyclic flow (PS I only) gives ATP only.
Chemiosmosis: protons accumulate in the lumen and ATP is made as they flow out through $CF_0$-$CF_1$.
Calvin cycle: carboxylation, reduction, regeneration; 6 turns, 18 ATP and 12 NADPH per glucose.
C4 pathway: PEPcase in mesophyll forms OAA, which goes as malate to the bundle sheath, where RuBisCO and the Calvin cycle work; there is no photorespiration.
Photorespiration: RuBP plus $O_2$ gives PGA plus phosphoglycolate and wastes energy.
Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm and gives net 2 ATP; the TCA cycle occurs in the matrix; ETS is on the inner mitochondrial membrane.
NADH gives 3 ATP and $FADH_2$ gives 2 ATP; aerobic respiration gives 38 ATP and fermentation gives 2 ATP.
RQ is 1 for carbohydrates, 0.7 for fats, 0.9 for proteins and infinite for anaerobic respiration.
Growth equations: $L_t = L_0 + rt$ (arithmetic) and $W_1 = W_0 e^{rt}$ (geometric, sigmoid curve).
Cell development: division, plasmatic growth, expansion, differentiation, maturation, senescence.
PGR roles: auxin for rooting and apical dominance, GA for bolting and malting, cytokinin for cell division, ethylene for ripening, ABA for dormancy and stomatal closure.
